In 2023, Australia amended our existing thin capitalisation (asset-based) rules to introduce an earnings-based rule, in line with the OECD Action 4. The amendment included two separate rules. The primary rule is the earnings-based rule - fixed ratio test - which applies to defined 'general entities'. This rule is agnostic to the source of debt. However, a targeted integrity rule - the debt deduction creation rule – operates to limit an entity’s ability to use related-party debt deductions to reduce their tax liability under the fixed ratio test. The secondary rule - the third-party debt test - applies to the same defined 'general entities' but targets entities investing in economic projects with long investment horizons, such as infrastructure and property. This test operates as a credit assessment test and denies the deductibility of any related party debt. Eligibility criteria limits this rule to third-party debt deductions used to fund commercial activity in Australia.
The debt deduction creation rule does not apply to authorised deposit-taking institutions, securitisation vehicles and certain special purposes entities. Authorised deposit-taking institutions (i.e. banks), financial entities, and Australian plantation forestry entities continue to be subject to the previous thin capitalisation rules.

Australian plantation forestry entities can claim interest deductions on debt up to the maximum of three tests: 

Statutory safe harbour debt limit: a set rate of debt that an entity can use to fund its Australian operations (60 per cent debt-to-total Australian assets). 

Arm’s length debt limit: this limit seeks to benchmark commercial or truly independent debt outcomes for the Australian operations. 

Worldwide gearing ratio test: this allows gearing of the Australian operations to be geared up to the level of the worldwide group. 

This reflects that this sector has unique harvesting timelines that result in long lead-times for earnings. 

There are also specific safe harbours for banks (authorised deposit-taking institutions) and financial entities – benchmarked to Basel III in 2014: 

ADI safe harbour: minimum 6 per cent risk weighted assets. 

Financials safe harbour: 93.75 per cent debt to assets (15:1 on debt-to-equity basis).
The worldwide gearing ratio test allows gearing of the Australian operations to be geared up to the level of the worldwide group.

The interest limitation rule (ILR) is a fixed ratio rule that links a company’s allowable net interest deductions directly to its level of economic activity. This is based on the company’s taxable earnings before deducting net interest expense, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA). 

The ILR defers the deductibility of interest until such time as the taxpayer has sufficient earnings to allow the deduction for interest. The ILR imposes a restriction on deductible net interest expense up to a limit of 30% of a taxpayer's tax EBITDA.

The ILR implements Article 4 of Council Directive (EU) 2016/1164 of 12 July 2016 (as amended) (‘ATAD’).

In line with ATAD, the ILR allows a higher percentage of a company’s tax EBITDA to be treated as a deductible interest expense by reference to the indebtedness of the worldwide group to which the taxpayer belongs. This is in recognition that some industries are more highly leveraged than others.  The percentage is calculated by expressing the group net interest expense as a percentage of group EBITDA. Where this is greater than 30%, the percentage can be substituted into the calculation of the allowable amount of net interest expense for the taxpayer.

In general, interest expense is only deductible where it meets certain conditions and can be broadly divided into five categories (each with their own specific criteria), these are: 1. Interest as a trading expense, 2. Interest as a deduction against rental income, 3. Interest as a charge on income, 4. Interest incurred by certain qualifying financing companies, and 5. Interest as a deduction against capital gains. These conditions apply before the application of the ILR.

With regard to the ILR, there are targeted anti-avoidance rules which apply to prevent the abuse of certain reliefs from the application of the ILR. In addition, there are rules to cater for the different tax rates that apply to trading income, passive income and capital gains to ensure that the interest to EBITDA test is applied uniformly to the tax value of the interest deduction.

Non-deductible interest expense may not be carried back. Non-deductible interest expense may be carried forward indefinitely to future accounting periods, where it may be deducted if the taxpayer has sufficient spare capacity in that period. A taxpayer’s spare capacity may be carried forward for a period of 60 months from the end of the accounting period in which it arose.

In addition to the interest limitation rule under Article 168bis LITL, Luxembourg’s framework is reinforced by the application of the arm’s length principle (Article 56 LITL and general transfer pricing rules) as well as by specific anti-abuse provisions applicable to transactions with associated enterprises resident in non-cooperative jurisdictions for tax purposes. These complementary measures further strengthen the integrity of the system and limit the scope for base erosion through excessive interest deductions.

Those not deductible financing expenses can be however deductible during the 5 (five) following taxation periods after net financing expenses of that period are considered, subject to the said limits, and if the net financing expenses is less than 30% of the EBITDA the unused part of this limit adds to this maximum deductible amount until the fifth following period of taxation.
